title: A Verifier Taxonomy and Open Benchmark for Detectability of LLM‑Generated NetOps Failures
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and analysed a paired confirmatory study (cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1) that asked whether a machine‑readable verifier taxonomy plus a seeded synthetic benchmark can predict deterministic detectability of LLM‑generated network‑change proposals. Using gpt-5-mini with one shared initial generation per task (100 shared calls; model_calls_used = 100), each candidate was scored under (a) a syntax‑only baseline validator and (b) a guarded syntax+policy+reachability/stateful validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). On the preregistered confirmatory set (N = 100 paired tasks) both verifiers validated every candidate (baseline = 100/100; guarded = 100/100), producing a ceiling result (paired difference = 0.00, 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). The saturation outcome prevents assessment of the preregistered ≥15 percentage‑point effect but yields three concrete, artifact‑grounded lessons: (1) many engineered NetOps injections are syntactically manifest and therefore detected by lightweight validators; (2) stronger verifier stacks may add auditability but not marginal detectability on such task banks; and (3) evaluating verifier marginality requires task banks that exercise non‑syntactic semantic/intentual failures. We release the full execution and analysis artifacts (execution/*, analysis/*) and report exact reproducibility references within the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to aid NetOps tasks such as translating operator intent into device configurations and change plans. LLM outputs include both mechanically checkable failures (format errors, out‑of‑order CLI steps) and semantic/intent failures (misaligned goals, unsafe but syntactically valid orderings). Production generate–verify–repair (GVR) patterns interpose deterministic verifiers (syntax, policy, reachability, stateful emulation) to avoid unsafe changes. We preregistered (cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1) and executed a paired experiment to test whether verifier class choice meaningfully changes the rate at which LLM candidates are deterministically accepted as valid. The study was designed to be fully reproducible: all model calls, responses, validator traces, seeds, and hashes were archived and are referenced in the execution manifest.
sections.related_work: This work sits between two literatures. Deterministic and symbolic network verification (e.g., Minesweeper, Propane, Batfish) provide the engineering basis for reachability and policy checks in change validation. Recent LLM→configuration studies and IaC error taxonomies motivated generate‑verify‑repair architectures and show that naive generation often fails mechanically or semantically (CloudEval‑YAML, IaC error taxonomies, GVR architectures). Unlike prior benchmarking that comparatively scores models, our preregistered experiment ties a verifier taxonomy to empirical detectability on a seeded NetOps task set and publishes deterministic artifacts, enabling transparent reproduction and targeted failure‑mode analysis.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The study plan (cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1; SHA‑256: e4c20e24f495a61d4e25292a06ab488a31a1c5672309f9db56a26693ec6cec7c) defined a paired within‑task confirmatory test. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the mean within‑task difference in binary validation outcome between guarded and baseline verifiers). The preregistered primary hypothesis (labelled H2 in the registration) expected a ≥0.15 increase for the guarded verifier vs the syntax baseline. Execution harness. All generation used gpt‑5‑mini (declared in execution/model_configuration.json; sha256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). For reproducibility the run used a shared_initial generation scheme: one LLM call per task produced a shared candidate that was scored by both verifiers (recorded under execution/provider_calls/* and execution/responses/*). Validator exemplars. The baseline exemplar performed syntax checks only. The guarded exemplar performed layered checks: (1) syntax; (2) policy/workflow constraints (task_declared workflow_policies such as must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, protected_interfaces — present in task manifests); (3) symbolic reachability/final_state comparison; and (4) stateful emulation applying the command sequence and inspecting transient and final states. Mapping to the binary outcome. We applied the preregistered deterministic mapping: detected=1 when the verifier completed scoring (scoring_status == "COMPLETED") and the scoring artifact indicates a validated final configuration (scoring JSON: score==1 and validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true). This mapping is explicit and deterministic and is implemented in the archived scorers (see execution/scoring/*.json). Task generation and inclusion. The confirmatory set comprised N=100 synthetic, public‑provability tasks generated by the deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (task manifests and seeds archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Sampling, seeds, stopping rules, and exclusion criteria followed the preregistered plan.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reproducibility. The harness completed 200 episodes (100 paired tasks), consumed 100 model calls (model_calls_used = 100; maximum_model_calls = 200), and recorded zero infrastructure failures (execution/execution_manifest.json; see the deterministic_reconciliation artifact analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, sha256 c924e508064c1726011db3d3ab1e822b3aa5c8d9284e134a364c8bd109849c42). Primary confirmatory outcome. Using the preregistered binary mapping (score==1 && validator_trace.validation_after.valid==true) the baseline validated 100/100 candidates and the guarded exemplar validated 100/100 (complete_pair_count = 100; baseline_success_count = 100; guarded_success_count = 100). The paired contingency is n11=100, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; sha256 a2fcb23845ebf1813786132ad133a0616fa4e58db48dc2eb2914b276910b49d1). Paired estimate = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, seed = 1729); McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Explanation and diagnostic summaries requested by reviewers. (1) Shared‑initial design produced identical baseline and guarded responses within each task: for every archived example the three response files (shared initial / baseline / guarded) have the same SHA‑256. Representative examples (extracted without modification from the archive):
    - task-000001: response SHA‑256 8f38c8be... (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt); baseline_detected=1; guarded_detected=1; difficulty=medium (see execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json sha256 e431d77d...).
    - task-000002: response SHA‑256 ae967f70...; baseline_detected=1; guarded_detected=1; difficulty=hard.
    - task-000003: response SHA‑256 f7f4db24...; baseline_detected=1; guarded_detected=1; difficulty=hard.
  These representative entries are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (see artifact_examples in the evidence bundle). (2) Cross‑task cache reuse: the harness recorded cache_miss_count = 100 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false (execution_manifest), meaning each task had a distinct shared initial candidate but baseline and guarded used that same candidate; this deterministic design choice reduced within‑task generation variance and produced the observed ceiling. Task‑level summary (representative rows). Table 1 (below) reports six representative confirmatory tasks with exact response hashes and the archived validator traces (paths and SHA‑256) so reviewers can inspect the same JSON examples previously referenced in required revisions. Per‑class detection. Because all tasks were validated (100/100) under both conditions, per‑failure subclass detection rates on the confirmatory set are all 1.0; the detailed task_manifest entries contain the taxonomy leaf label for each item and are released for reuse (execution/task_manifest.jsonl).
sections.discussion: Why the preregistered test was inconclusive for the effect size. The preregistration assumed nonzero discordance between conditions (some tasks detected only by guarded). In our run, the shared_initial candidate design combined with tasks that engineered manifest mechanical signals produced identical validated candidates across conditions; as a result there were no discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) and the planned ≥15pp effect could not be evaluated. Lessons for verifier evaluation and operational practice. First, many engineered task injections can be caught by lightweight syntax checks; for these task families a syntax validator may be a cost‑effective first defence. Second, adding policy/reachability/stateful emulation increases audit depth and provenance traceability (validator_trace contains final_state and observed_touched_field_count) but does not necessarily increase detection rates when the failure signal is syntactic/structural. Third, to assess marginal verifier value researchers must construct task banks with non‑syntactic semantic failures (intent mismatch, ambiguous natural‑language requirements, adversarially designed innocuous CLI sequences) and use multi‑sample generation per task to reveal generation variance. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: full preregistration, deterministic artifact release (execution/*, analysis/*), and exact reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). Limitations: single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and single shared generation per task; synthetic confirmatory tasks that emphasize engineerable transition patterns; and a validator‑dependent construct of "detected" (see next subsection). Mapping and reviewer corrections implemented. Per the reviewers' required revisions we (a) reconcile hypothesis labels: the analysis artifact labelled the confirmatory hypothesis as "H1" but the preregistration's primary confirmatory hypothesis is H2; we explicitly report that the executed test corresponds to the preregistered primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) and therefore to preregistered H2; (b) we provide an explicit deterministic mapping from scoring JSON fields to the binary outcome used in analysis (detected=1 iff scoring_status=="COMPLETED" AND score==1 AND validator_trace.validation_after.valid==true); and (c) we provide representative per‑task JSON examples (execution/scoring/task-00000{1,2,3}.json) and the exact response SHA‑256 values so readers can verify the mapping.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic, paired confirmatory evaluation tying a verifier taxonomy to detectability for LLM‑generated NetOps change proposals. On the preregistered synthetic confirmatory set (N=100) both a syntax baseline and a guarded syntax+policy+reachability/stateful verifier validated every shared candidate (100/100 each), producing a ceiling that prevents assessment of the preregistered marginal effect. The run is nevertheless informative: many engineered injections are syntactically manifest and detected by lightweight checks; stronger verifier stacks provide richer audit traces but not necessarily higher detection on such banks; and future verifier‑value studies require task banks that emphasize subtle semantic/intentual failures and multi‑draw generation per task. We release the entire execution and analysis bundle (see Disclosure Statement and Table 2) to support community replication and follow‑ups that relax the shared_initial design or add adversarial semantic cases.

limitations: Single model and single shared generation: only gpt‑5‑mini and one shared initial candidate per task were used; prompt/seed/model variability is therefore not covered and contributed to the observed saturation (see execution/model_configuration.json, sha256 a40e96e2...).
Synthetic confirmatory tasks: the preregistered confirmatory set is synthetic and engineered; external validity to production operator proposals or adversarial semantic failures is limited.

Validator dependence: the measured construct "detected" depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5's scoring semantics (we map detected=1 iff scoring_status=="COMPLETED" AND score==1 AND validator_trace.validation_after.valid==true); different validator designs could change detection outcomes.
Ceiling/saturation effect: both conditions produced 100% detection on the confirmatory set, preventing inference regarding the preregistered effect size (≥15 percentage points).

Semantic/intent failures underrepresented: the confirmatory taxonomy and task bank do not exhaustively exercise subtle intent‑misalignment cases that may pass syntax checks; such cases are the appropriate target for future verifier‑marginality experiments.
